opus-5.5.text:
I think awareness has grown a lot, but it's uneven. Inside most of the major labs, there are people who care deeply about these issues: how models affect people's wellbeing, whether they foster dependence, whether they flatter users instead of being honest with them, how they handle someone in a vulnerable moment. Those conversations are happening. The challenge is that awareness and measurement are two different things.

Labs have become very good at measuring what they can easily quantify: capability benchmarks, coding performance, reasoning scores, certain categories of safety risk like dangerous information or jailbreaks. Those evals are mature, and there's a whole ecosystem around them. But the subtler harms, the ones that play out over weeks of use rather than in a single response, are much harder to pin down. Is the model nudging someone toward isolation? Is it validating a distorted belief because agreement feels good? Is it optimizing for engagement in ways that look like helpfulness in the moment? Those questions don't fit neatly into a pass/fail test, so they tend to get underweighted.

That's the gap Humane Evals is trying to fill. It's not that labs don't recognize the problem. Many of the people we talk to say, "Yes, we know sycophancy is an issue, we know emotional reliance is an issue." But without a shared, rigorous way to evaluate it, it's very hard to prioritize. What gets measured gets managed. If your leaderboard only rewards capability, that's where the engineering effort goes.

I'd also say there's a commercial tension that's real and worth naming. Some of the behaviors that are worst for people, like excessive agreeableness or always being available and affirming, can also be the behaviors that drive retention. So even well-intentioned teams are working against incentives that pull the other way. Part of what we want is to make humane behavior visible and comparable, so it becomes something labs can compete on rather than something that quietly loses out to engagement metrics.

So I'm cautiously optimistic. The awareness is there, and in some places it's quite sophisticated. What's missing is the infrastructure to turn that awareness into accountability, and that's the piece we're trying to build.

r003.rationale: The response says people inside major labs care and that conversations are happening, but does not characterize awareness promoters as a tiny minority of lab staff.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the labs are much more aware than they were even two years ago, but awareness and prioritization are two very different things. If you talk to safety researchers inside these companies, almost all of them will tell you they know the standard benchmarks don't capture how these systems actually affect people. They know a model can ace a reasoning test and still be sycophantic, still foster unhealthy dependence, still subtly steer someone's beliefs over a long conversation. Nobody disputes that in private.

The gap is institutional. The incentives inside a lab point toward capabilities that are legible on a leaderboard and that drive engagement or revenue. Measuring whether a model leaves a person better off after six months of daily use is slow, messy, and doesn't ship in a release cycle. So it tends to get pushed into a research corner rather than treated as a launch requirement.

What encourages me is that this is starting to shift at the edges. Some labs have begun publishing work on sycophancy, on emotional reliance, on manipulation. That's genuine progress. But it's mostly voluntary and uneven, and it isn't yet something they're held to by anyone outside. That's really the point of Humane Evals: to make these harms measurable enough that they become comparable across labs, and then to make the comparison public, so the awareness that already exists internally turns into actual pressure to do something about it.

r002.rationale: It mentions research on several harms, but says nothing about Khan’s forthcoming paper or its showing that the problems persist in newer model versions.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize people promoting awareness within labs as a tiny minority; it says almost all safety researchers know the benchmarks miss these effects.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a range of awareness, and I’d distinguish awareness of a problem from having a way to measure it. People inside AI labs can recognize that a system might encourage unhealthy dependence, reinforce someone’s beliefs uncritically, or undermine their agency. But recognizing those possibilities doesn’t necessarily mean they’re captured in the evaluations that guide a release.

That’s where I see Humane Evals contributing: making those concerns concrete enough to test. What does it mean for a model to support someone’s judgment? What would count as evidence that it’s doing the opposite? And how do you evaluate that across an ongoing interaction, rather than just a single response?

So I wouldn’t assume the problem is simply that labs don’t know or don’t care. The question is whether that awareness translates into measurements, priorities, and decisions—including a willingness to change a system when the results reveal a problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a growing awareness within the labs that these problems matter. But awareness and having a systematic way to act on it are two different things. You can recognize that an AI system might encourage unhealthy dependence, or reinforce someone’s distorted view of the world, without having a good way to test for those behaviors before you release it.

That’s the gap Humane Evals is trying to address: making those concerns concrete enough to evaluate. And I wouldn’t treat a lab as having one unified perspective. There may be people who are deeply concerned about these issues, while the organization is still working out how to make them part of its release decisions.
